newsitem.title: UK: Dollar profits as French poll stokes EMU nerves.
newsitem.headline: Dollar profits as French poll stokes EMU nerves.

text.p: The dollar was cruising at four-week peaks against the mark at European midsession as the left-wing victory in France's parliamentary election sent players swarming into perceived safe havens.

With the French Socialists reliant on the Communists to form a government and pledging a Europe without austerity, analysts said the market was now fretting that this implied either delay to economic and monetary union or a broad-based, soft euro.
"Neither of those will be palatable to the European bloc -- near-term it seems the dollar is the winner," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International.
The dollar romped to 1.7218/25 marks by 1106 GMT from 1.7082/92 in late Europe on Friday.
Analysts said the mark was supported to a degree by talk of EMU delay, but even that support was limited as weakening satellite currencies would hit Germany's export performance.
That would provide an unfavourable contrast with the current health of the U.S. economy, to dollar/mark's advantage, said Peter Wood, forex trader at Bank of Boston here.
"At the end of the day the U.S. economy is going great guns...the likelihood is we might get higher U.S. interest rates if anything, so I don't see a major outflow of dollars."

Fears of a broad, weak European single currency were fuelled by French Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande, who called for Italy and Spain to be included in EMU and said all stood to benefit if the euro "no longer means austerity".

"The French election results have increased the prospect of a softer euro. That is clearly bad news for the deutschmark, and clearly the dollar has benefited," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International here.
Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said the EMU project may enter "rougher waters" in months ahead, and said it would become clear in coming weeks whether the euro would be stable.

Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet insisted, however, that the euro would and must have the legacy of the most solid ERM currencies, and said EMU would foster structural reform and promote growth in Europe.

Analysts were unconvinced. "Europe as a collective against the rest of the world is sending out the message it's going to devalue itself relative to the dollar and the yen and sterling to get itself out of trouble and reflate itself," said Chris Tinker, chief treasury economist at Standard Chartered here.
Sterling stormed ahead with its U.S. counterpart, rising to 2.8160/70 marks by 1146 GMT from late Friday's 2.7960/75.
Dollar/yen was sidelined but edged up to 116.62/72 from 116.37/47 at Friday's close.
Despite the market's focus on Europe, the U.S. will offer plenty of food for thought this week as players await the release of May non-farm payrolls on Friday.

Today sees the release of U.S. April personal income and spending figures at 1230 GMT, but more important will be the May National Association of Purchasing Managers index at 1400 GMT, seen easing to 53.9 from 54.2 last time. The employment component will be a key market pointer ahead of payrolls, analysts said.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to 5.8170/90 French francs from late Friday's 5.7690/20 and 1.4345/55 Swiss francs from 1.4145/55.
